transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hello, Doctor. Thank you so much for taking the time to see me. I, um... I hope I'm doing this right, I've never really been to a clinic like this before. 

Well, I suppose I'm here because I've been having a bit of a... a hiccup, lately. My wife had a fall recently, and... well, I’ve always been the man with the lists and the plan, you know? I like to keep things organized and handle my responsibilities. But since her fall, I'm a little embarrassed to admit this, and I hope you don't judge me too harshly for it... I've just been spending hours sitting at the kitchen table, just staring at her medication chart. 

I've been a bit overly emotional, maybe shedding a tear here and there, or snapping over absolutely nothing, which isn't like me at all. And I’ve sort of let things slip. The bills, my mentoring calls, even just basic housework... it's all piling up. I just feel like I can’t make myself function the way I ought to right now. 

Does that make sense? I'm trying my best, I really am, I just... I wanted to see if maybe you could tell me if this is a normal way to react?
Have you noticed that you’re not enjoying things that you usually like doing, like maybe hobbies, mentoring calls, or even simple routines around the house?

Well, yes... you've, um, you've hit the nail right on the head there. I feel a bit dreadful admitting this, because I've always prided myself on being reliable, you know? I hope you don't think less of me for it, but... I’ve actually stopped showing up for my mentoring calls. And my other community commitments, too. I just... I haven't had it in me, and I feel terrible because I know I'm letting people down. 

And around the house... well, it's exactly as you said. Things I used to handle without even thinking twice about them—paying the bills on time, the general home upkeep, just the basic daily routines—they're really slipping badly right now. I try to get to them, I really do, but I just end up back at that kitchen table. 

Is it normal to just completely lose your grip on these everyday things when you're worried like this? I just want to make sure I'm explaining it properly, and giving you the right picture of what's going on.

Over the past couple of weeks, have you noticed a change in your energy levels—like feeling more tired than usual or finding it harder to get through the day, even if you haven’t done much physically?

Well, um... actually, no. I don't think I've noticed anything quite like that. I hope I'm not being unhelpful by saying this, but my physical energy seems... well, it seems perfectly fine. 

I'm not really feeling exhausted or needing to lie down during the day, thankfully. I still feel physically capable of doing things, which is, I suppose, why I feel so foolish that I'm just... not getting them done. It's more that I just get stuck sitting there worrying at the table, rather than feeling too physically tired to move. 

Does that make sense? I just want to be sure I'm answering your questions correctly so I'm not wasting your time.
Have you found that activities you used to enjoy, like mentoring or community work, feel less interesting or rewarding to you now?

Well, um... I wouldn't say they feel less interesting or rewarding, exactly. I still care about the young men I mentor, very much so. I hope it doesn't sound like I've just stopped caring about them, because I haven't. 

It's just... I suppose my mind is just so preoccupied with my wife and making sure I don't mess up her medications that I just can't seem to focus on those other things right now. It's not that I don't want to do them or don't find them fulfilling anymore, it's just that I can't seem to pull myself away from the kitchen table to actually do them. 

Does that make a difference? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right information. I'm not depressed or anything like that, I just... I'm just a bit stuck right now, I think.

The lack of anhedonia, preserved energy levels, and the context of recent stressor (wife's fall) support adjustment disorder (F43.22) rather than depressive disorder (F32.1).
